title: Reporting: verbs, patterns and distance
tagline: Every reporting verb has its own grammar — get it right, and 'he said that' stops sounding flat.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (DENIED, INSISTED, ACCUSED, DISSUADED, CLAIMS, WHETHER)
Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze
Writing Part 2 — article/report: attributing claims responsibly
Speaking Part 3 — reporting group disagreements accurately
why: Reporting is more than 'he said that…': each reporting verb has its own grammar — deny + -ing, insist + that, accuse + of — and choosing the wrong pattern is a classic C1 slip. Hedged reporting (claim, allege, is thought to) also lets a writer distance themselves from a claim, which examiners and journalists both value.

Structure
Example

Miss Vega urged them to submit the draft early.

use.point: Reporting verbs with their own patterns

examples.text: He denied copying the answer from his classmate.
She insisted that the deadline be extended for everyone.
The coach threatened to cancel the match if the noise continued.
They accused him of copying the essay word for word.
She blamed the printer for ruining her assignment.
Her parents dissuaded her from dropping the subject.

use.point: Hedged reporting: claim, allege, is said/thought to

examples.text: The article alleges that the results were manipulated.
examples.note: allege, more formal than claim, often unproven

examples.text: He claims to have read the entire syllabus overnight.
The manuscript is thought to date back several centuries.

use.point: Reported questions, no backshift, and summarising

examples.text: She asked whether the results had been published yet.
He said the school is the oldest in the region.
In short, Miss Vega told them to revise their bibliography and resubmit.

watch_out.wrong: He denied that he copy the answer.
watch_out.why: Deny takes an -ing form or a correctly tensed that-clause, not a bare infinitive.

watch_out.wrong: She insisted to extend the deadline.
watch_out.right: She insisted that the deadline be extended.
watch_out.why: Insist is followed by a that-clause (with should/subjunctive), not a to-infinitive.
Accuse takes of; blame takes for — the two prepositions are not interchangeable.

watch_out.wrong: Her parents dissuaded her to drop the subject.
watch_out.right: Her parents dissuaded her from dropping the subject.
watch_out.why: Dissuade takes from + -ing, not to + infinitive.

watch_out.wrong: He claims that he has reading the whole book.
watch_out.right: He claims to have read the whole book.
watch_out.why: A perfect infinitive needs have + past participle, not have + -ing.

watch_out.wrong: She asked did the results come out yet.
watch_out.right: She asked whether the results had come out yet.
watch_out.why: Reported questions use normal word order and whether/if, never the original question form.

dialogue.title: Setting the record straight
dialogue.context: After a mix-up during the mock exam, Liam and Nadia report to Miss Vega exactly what different people said and did.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Before I write the incident report, tell me exactly what happened, please.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Well, Mr Ramos accused Mateo of talking during the silent reading section.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: But Mateo denied talking — he said he was only pointing at the clock.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: And what did Mateo say when Mr Ramos confronted him?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: He insisted that he hadn't said a single word.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Sofia, who sits nearby, claims to have seen the whole thing, and she agrees with Mateo.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Did anyone try to calm the situation down?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Yes — the invigilator urged everyone to stay quiet and keep working.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Mr Ramos later blamed the confusion on the poor lighting, not on Mateo directly.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: And Mateo — did he threaten to complain, or anything like that?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: No, he just threatened to ask for a seat change next time, nothing dramatic.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good. In short, then, nobody should be blamed for anything — it was a genuine misunderstanding.

items.sentence: He ___ copying the answer from his neighbour.
items.why: Deny is followed directly by an -ing form (or a that-clause), never a to-infinitive.

items.sentence: She ___ that the deadline be extended for everyone.
items.why: Insist + that-clause (with should/subjunctive) expresses a firm demand.

items.sentence: They ___ him of copying the essay.
items.why: Accuse + object + of + -ing is the fixed pattern.

items.sentence: She ___ the printer for ruining her assignment.
Her parents ___ her from dropping the subject.
items.why: Dissuade + object + from + -ing is the pattern for talking someone out of something.

items.sentence: He ___ to have read the entire syllabus overnight.
items.why: Claim + perfect infinitive (to have + participle) hedges a boastful statement.

items.sentence: She asked ___ the results had been published yet.
items.why: Reported yes/no questions use whether/if + normal word order, not inversion.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between two and five words.

items.first: 'I didn't copy the answer,' said Mateo.
'The deadline really must be extended,' said Sofia firmly.
The teacher said Mateo copied the essay.
Her parents persuaded her not to drop the subject.
He says he read the entire syllabus overnight, apparently.
People think the manuscript dates back centuries.
'Have the results come out yet?' she wanted to know.

summary: Reporting verbs carry their own grammar: deny + -ing, insist + that, threaten/refuse/offer + to-infinitive.
Accuse … of, blame … for and dissuade … from all take object + preposition + -ing.
Hedge a claim with claim/allege + that or is said/thought to when you can't confirm it.
Backshift the tense when reporting after a past verb, unless the fact is still true or very recent.
A good summary reports the gist — who said, asked or urged what — not every original word.
